title: Leviathan; or, The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill
description: Hobbes's masterwork of political philosophy, in which the commonwealth is conceived as an artificial man whose soul is sovereignty, founded on a covenant by which individuals transfer their right of self-government to an absolute sovereign.
plot_or_argument: Part I ('Of Man') sets out Hobbes's materialist psychology and his state of nature, in which life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; part II ('Of Common-Wealth') derives the sovereign's absolute authority from the social contract; part III ('Of a Christian Common-Wealth') subordinates the church to the state; part IV ('Of the Kingdom of Darkness') attacks scholastic and papal claims.
narrative_structure: Four parts in 47 numbered chapters, with the famous engraved frontispiece of the giant sovereign composed of his subjects.
meter_and_prosody: A powerful, lucid English prose deliberately free of rhetorical ornament; Hobbes's style became a model of the plain philosophical sentence.
historical_context: Composed in Paris during Hobbes's exile and published in London in 1651, two years after the execution of Charles I; it was condemned by royalists and by Presbyterians alike and was later attacked in Parliament as an encouragement to atheism.
literary_significance: The foundational text of modern political philosophy and of social contract theory; it transformed the vocabulary of politics, founded the modern theory of sovereignty, and provoked responses from Locke, Rousseau, and every subsequent theorist of the state.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Hobbes; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1651 (Andrew Crooke, London); Latin edition 1668. Standard edition: Leviathan: The English and Latin Texts (Noel Malcolm, ed., Clarendon Press, 2012), 3 vols.

title: De Cive
alternative_titles: Philosophical Rudiments Concerning Government and Society
description: Hobbes's first published statement of his political theory, the third part of his philosophical system, which argues from the state of nature to the necessity of an absolute sovereign and was published in Latin in Paris in 1642.
plot_or_argument: In three parts — Libertas (the state of nature), Imperium (the establishment of government), and Religio (the kingdom of God) — Hobbes derives the sovereign's absolute authority from the natural right of self-preservation.
narrative_structure: Eighteen chapters in three sections.
meter_and_prosody: Latin philosophical prose; translated into English as Philosophical Rudiments in 1651.
historical_context: Published at Paris in April 1642, on the eve of the English civil wars, which Hobbes said determined his subject; expanded edition 1647.
literary_significance: The prototype of Leviathan and the first full modern statement of social contract theory; its influence on seventeenth-century political thought was immediate and enormous.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Hobbes; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published Paris, 1642; Amsterdam edition 1647. Standard edition: De Cive: The English Version (Howard Warrender, ed., Oxford University Press, 1983); Elementa Philosophica de Cive (H. Warrender, ed., Clarendon Press, 1983).

title: The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic
description: Hobbes's first systematic treatise, circulated in manuscript in 1640 and dedicated to the Earl of Newcastle, which was published without his consent in 1650 in two separately titled parts.
plot_or_argument: Part I ('Human Nature') sets out Hobbes's materialist psychology; part II ('De Corpore Politico') derives the necessity of government from the state of nature and defends absolute sovereignty.
narrative_structure: Two parts, each subdivided into chapters; the 1650 printing divided them into separate books.
meter_and_prosody: Plain argumentative prose.
historical_context: Circulated in manuscript in 1640 during the Short Parliament; Hobbes fled to Paris in November 1640 as the treatise's royalism became dangerous.
literary_significance: The first statement of Hobbes's system and a crucial document of the intellectual origins of the civil-war controversy on sovereignty.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Hobbes; the manuscript circulated under his name and the 1650 printing was unauthorised.
bibliographical_notes: Manuscript 1640; first printed 1650 as Human Nature and De Corpore Politico. Standard edition: The Elements of Law (J. C. A. Gaskin, ed., Oxford University Press, 1994).

title: Behemoth; or, The Long Parliament
description: Hobbes's history of the English civil wars in the form of a dialogue, written in old age as a companion to Leviathan and suppressed by Charles II, but printed without authority in 1679 and after Hobbes's death in 1682.
plot_or_argument: In four dialogues between A and B, Hobbes explains the causes of the civil wars as the spread of seditious doctrines from the Presbyterians, the Independents, and the universities, and the ambition of the parliamentary leaders.
narrative_structure: Four dialogues covering 1640 to 1660.
principal_characters: A (the narrator); B (the questioner); Charles I; Cromwell; the Long Parliament
meter_and_prosody: Conversational prose dialogue.
historical_context: Written c. 1668-70; Charles II refused permission to publish it, and it appeared in an unauthorised edition in 1679 and an authorised edition in 1682.
literary_significance: Hobbes's own interpretation of the events that produced Leviathan and a key text for understanding his theory of sedition and the role of universities and clergy in politics.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Hobbes; the 1679 edition was unauthorised and Hobbes complained of its errors.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1679 (unauthorised); authorised edition 1682. Standard edition: Behemoth (Paul Seaward, ed., Clarendon Press, 2010).

title: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding
description: Locke's founding work of modern empiricism, an enquiry into the origin, certainty, and extent of human knowledge, which rejects innate ideas and argues that all thought derives from sensation and reflection.
plot_or_argument: Book I refutes innate ideas; book II sets out the theory of simple and complex ideas derived from sensation and reflection; book III treats the philosophy of language and the abuse of words; book IV defines knowledge and probability and examines the grounds of belief.
narrative_structure: Four books in a systematic argument of 71 chapters.
meter_and_prosody: A clear, deliberate, sometimes conversational prose; Locke's plain style was consciously opposed to scholastic Latinism.
historical_context: Begun in 1671 in discussion with friends including James Tyrrell, completed during Locke's exile in Holland, and published in December 1689 (dated 1690) after the Revolution.
literary_significance: The founding text of British empiricism and of the Enlightenment theory of mind; it shaped Berkeley, Hume, and Kant, and its influence on eighteenth-century literature, psychology, and educational theory was pervasive.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Locke; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1689 (title dated 1690); fourth edition 1700 with Locke's additions. Standard edition: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (Peter H. Nidditch, ed., Clarendon Press, 1975).

title: Two Treatises of Government
alternative_titles: Two Treatises of Government: In the Latter, the False Principles and Foundation of Sir Robert Filmer and His Followers are Detected and Overthrown
description: Locke's classic of liberal political theory, published anonymously in 1689, which refutes Filmer's divine-right absolutism and sets out a theory of government founded on natural rights, consent, property, and the right of resistance.
plot_or_argument: The First Treatise demolishes Filmer's Patriarcha chapter by chapter; the Second Treatise argues that political power derives from the consent of free and equal individuals who form a society to protect their natural rights to life, liberty, and estate.
narrative_structure: Two treatises: the first a detailed refutation, the second a positive theory in 19 chapters.
meter_and_prosody: Vigorous argumentative prose with biblical and legal citation.
historical_context: Composed during the Exclusion Crisis of 1679-81, revised in Holland, and published anonymously in December 1689 (dated 1690) as a justification of the Revolution that brought William and Mary to the throne; Locke never acknowledged authorship.
literary_significance: The foundational text of modern liberalism and of the theory of limited constitutional government; it directly influenced the American Declaration of Independence and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; Locke's authorship was not publicly acknowledged in his lifetime but is established from his correspondence and papers.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1689/90. Standard edition: Two Treatises of Government (Peter Laslett, ed., Cambridge University Press, 1960; 3rd edn 1988).

title: A Letter Concerning Toleration
description: Locke's argument for religious toleration, written in Latin in Holland in 1685 and published anonymously in 1689 in William Popple's English translation; it separates the ends of civil government from the care of souls.
plot_or_argument: The magistrate's power extends only to civil interests — life, liberty, health, and property; the care of souls belongs to no one but God, and persecution cannot produce sincere belief; therefore the state must tolerate all religions that do not threaten civil peace.
narrative_structure: A single continuous letter addressed to an unnamed friend.
meter_and_prosody: Clear Latin prose, widely read in Popple's English translation.
historical_context: Written in 1685 after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, in correspondence with Philip van Limborch; published in 1689 at Gouda in the same year as the Revolution settlement.
literary_significance: The classic statement of the case for religious toleration and a foundational text of liberal pluralism; three further letters followed in 1690, 1692, and 1704.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously as Epistola de Tolerantia; the English translation was by William Popple; Locke's authorship was suspected but not acknowledged.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1689 (Gouda); English translation 1689. Standard edition: A Letter Concerning Toleration (James H. Tully, ed., Hackett, 1983); also in The Works of John Locke, vol. VI.

title: Some Thoughts Concerning Education
description: Locke's influential treatise on the education of a young gentleman, which grew out of letters to his friend Edward Clarke and argued for physical hardiness, moral habituation, and a practical curriculum over rote learning.
plot_or_argument: Locke advises on the health of the body, the formation of the mind through habit and example, the teaching of reading, writing, languages, history, geography, arithmetic, and a trade, and the importance of curiosity over coercion.
narrative_structure: A series of numbered sections following the natural order of education.
meter_and_prosody: Practical, conversational prose.
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1693, expanded in the 1695 and 1705 editions; it derived from Locke's letters to Edward Clarke of Chipley concerning Clarke's son.
literary_significance: The most influential English work on education of the eighteenth century; it shaped Rousseau's Emile, and its emphasis on habit and on the child's own interest transformed educational theory.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; authorship was publicly acknowledged only in the 1705 edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1693; fifth edition 1705. Standard edition: Some Thoughts Concerning Education (John W. Yolton and Jean S. Yolton, eds., Clarendon Press, 1989).

title: The Reasonableness of Christianity, as Delivered in the Scriptures
description: Locke's anonymously published theological treatise, which argues that the single necessary article of Christian faith is the belief that Jesus is the Messiah, and that reason and Scripture are in harmony.
plot_or_argument: Locke examines the Gospels and Epistles to show that the essential doctrine of Christianity is the messiahship of Jesus, and that this belief is both scripturally grounded and reasonable.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument following the narrative of the Gospels.
meter_and_prosody: Plain argumentative prose.
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1695, during the Trinitarian controversy, and attacked by John Edwards in Socinianism Unmask'd; Locke replied in Vindication of the Reasonableness of Christianity (1695).
literary_significance: A founding text of English rational religion and latitudinarian theology; its influence on the eighteenth-century debate on revelation and reason was profound, and it prepared the way for Deism and for Locke's own reputation as a rational Christian.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; authorship was widely suspected and acknowledged in the second edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1695; second edition 1695 with additions. Standard edition: The Reasonableness of Christianity (John C. Higgins-Biddle, ed., Clarendon Press, 1999).

title: The Sceptical Chymist
alternative_titles: The Sceptical Chymist; or, Chymico-Physical Doubts and Paradoxes
description: Robert Boyle's dialogue attacking the Aristotelian and Paracelsian theories of the elements, arguing for a corpuscular (mechanical) account of matter and insisting that chemical claims must be established by experiment.
plot_or_argument: In a dialogue among Carneades, Eleutherius, Philoponus, and Themistius, Boyle argues that neither the four Aristotelian elements nor the three Paracelsian principles can be demonstrated; only experiment can determine the composition of bodies.
narrative_structure: A dialogue in six parts with an appendix of experiments.
meter_and_prosody: Argumentative prose with detailed experimental description.
historical_context: Published in 1661, a year after the Restoration and the year before the Royal Society's charter; Boyle was a founding fellow and the leading experimental philosopher of the age.
literary_significance: The work that separated chemistry from alchemy and established it as an experimental science; its sceptical method and its corpuscularianism were decisive for the new philosophy.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Boyle; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1661; second edition 1680. Standard edition: The Works of the Honourable Robert Boyle (Thomas Birch, ed., 1772), vol. I; also Boyle's Sceptical Chymist (J. R. Partington, ed.).

title: New Experiments Physico-Mechanical, Touching the Spring of the Air
description: Boyle's report of his experiments with the air-pump built for him by Robert Hooke, in which he demonstrated the elastic 'spring' of air, its necessity for respiration and sound, and stated the inverse relation between pressure and volume now known as Boyle's Law.
plot_or_argument: Forty-three experiments establish the properties of the air and answer the objections of Hobbes and the Peripatetics; the famous Experiment 41 shows that a sound cannot be heard in an evacuated vessel.
narrative_structure: A series of numbered experiments with descriptions of apparatus, results, and objections answered.
meter_and_prosody: Detailed experimental prose; Boyle's practice of reporting full particulars became the model for the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions.
historical_context: Published in 1660 at Oxford, where Boyle worked with Hooke; the second edition of 1662 added the Defence of the Doctrine Touching the Spring and Weight of the Air, containing the pressure-volume relation.
literary_significance: The foundational text of modern experimental physics and chemistry; it established the experimental report as a literary form and Boyle's Law as the first quantitative gas law.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Boyle; Hooke built the apparatus and is credited in the text.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1660; second edition 1662. Standard edition: The Works of the Honourable Robert Boyle (Thomas Birch, ed., 1772); Robert Boyle's Experiments Physico-Mechanical (Michael Hunter and Edward B. Davis, eds.).

title: The Description of a New World, Called The Blazing-World
description: Margaret Cavendish's fantastical prose fiction, appended to her Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, in which a young lady is carried to a parallel world at the North Pole inhabited by hybrid animal-men and rules it as empress.
plot_or_argument: A lady is abducted, carried to the Blazing World, and made empress; she converses with the animal-men and with the soul of the Duchess of Newcastle about natural philosophy, then returns to rescue her native world from invasion.
narrative_structure: A two-part narrative of travel and philosophical dialogue, combining utopian fiction, romance, and natural philosophy.
principal_characters: the Empress; the Duchess of Newcastle; the Bear-men; the Bird-men; the Fish-men; the Ape-men; the Satyrs; the Worm-men
literary_form: utopian fiction; prose romance; science fiction; philosophical dialogue
meter_and_prosody: Vigorous, digressive prose of great imaginative freedom.
historical_context: Published in 1666 together with Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, as an appendix; Cavendish was living in exile and later visited the Royal Society in 1667, the first woman to do so.
literary_significance: The first science fiction by a woman in English, a pioneering work of utopian and speculative fiction, and a philosophical answer to the experimentalists; it has become a canonical text of early modern women's writing.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Cavendish; the title page names her as the Duchess of Newcastle.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1666. Standard edition: The Blazing World and Other Writings (Kate Lilley, ed., Penguin Classics, 1992); Paper Bodies: Early Utopian Fictions by Women (Sylvia Bowerbank and Sara Mendelson, eds., OUP, 2000).

title: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy
alternative_titles: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, to Which is Added The Description of a New Blazing World
description: Cavendish's philosophical critique of the new experimental philosophy, attacking the Royal Society's microscopy, Hooke's Micrographia, and the corpuscular theories of Hobbes, Descartes, and Boyle, and proposing her own vitalist materialism.
plot_or_argument: Cavendish argues that matter is self-moving, sentient, and rational; she rejects the mechanical philosophy's reliance on instruments, which she thought distorted nature, and asserts a holistic, animistic view of the natural world.
narrative_structure: A systematic critique in chapters, followed by the appendix The Blazing World.
meter_and_prosody: Argumentative prose of remarkable originality and density.
historical_context: Published in 1666; Cavendish was one of the few women to engage directly with the Royal Society, and her critique of Hooke's microscopy was a direct response to Micrographia (1665).
literary_significance: The most substantial philosophical work by an English woman of the seventeenth century and an important early critique of instrumental science; it has been revalued as a serious contribution to natural philosophy.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Cavendish; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1666. Standard edition: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (Eileen O'Neill, ed., Cambridge University Press, 2001).

title: Plays, Never Before Printed (Cavendish)
description: Cavendish's collection of dramatic works, written in exile and never performed, including comedies, tragicomedies, and closet plays that experiment with genre and defend female authorship.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains Loves Adventures, The Comical Hash, Youth's Glory and Death's Banquet, The Lady Contemplation, and others; The Convent of Pleasure, a separate 1668 publication, imagines a female community free of men.
narrative_structure: A collection of plays in mixed prose and verse, with prefaces defending the author's right to write.
principal_characters: Lady Happy (The Convent of Pleasure); Affectionata; Innocencia; various
meter_and_prosody: Mixed prose and verse.
historical_context: Published in 1662 while Cavendish was in exile with her husband William Cavendish, Duke of Newcastle; a second volume of plays appeared in 1668.
literary_significance: The largest body of drama by a seventeenth-century English woman and a pioneering experiment in the closet play; The Convent of Pleasure is a landmark of early feminist literature.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Cavendish; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1662; second volume 1668. Standard edition: The Convent of Pleasure and Other Plays (Anne Shaver, ed., Johns Hopkins University Press, 1999).

title: The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy
alternative_titles: The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy, Concerning God, Christ, and the Creatures
description: Anne Conway's philosophical treatise, written in the last years of her life and published posthumously in Latin in 1690 and in English in 1692; it proposes a monistic vitalist metaphysics in which all creatures are degrees of one spiritual substance.
plot_or_argument: In nine chapters Conway argues that God is infinitely good and communicative, that creatures are mutable spiritual substances capable of perfecting themselves, and that the dualism of Descartes and the materialism of Hobbes are both false.
narrative_structure: Nine chapters of systematic metaphysics.
meter_and_prosody: Scholarly philosophical prose.
historical_context: Composed c. 1679 while Conway suffered from chronic illness; published in Amsterdam in 1690 as Principia philosophiae antiquissimae and translated into English in 1692.
literary_significance: One of the most original philosophical works of the seventeenth century and the first by an English woman to be published as a systematic metaphysics; it influenced Leibniz and has been revalued as a major contribution to early modern philosophy.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Anne Conway, Viscountess Conway; authorship is established from the manuscript and the posthumous publication.
bibliographical_notes: Latin edition Amsterdam, 1690; English edition London, 1692. Standard edition: The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy (Allison P. Coudert and Taylor Corse, eds., Cambridge University Press, 1996).

title: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies, for the Advancement of Their True and Greatest Interest
alternative_titles: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies
description: Mary Astell's feminist treatise proposing a Protestant monastery or religious retirement where women could pursue education and the life of the mind free from marriage and male authority.
plot_or_argument: Part I (1694) argues that women's intellectual inferiority is the product of defective education and proposes a religious community for their instruction; part II (1697) supplies a method for the improvement of women's minds based on Cartesian clear and distinct ideas.
narrative_structure: Two parts, each a continuous argument with a prefatory dedication.
meter_and_prosody: Vigorous, ironic, and rhetorically accomplished prose.
historical_context: Part I published anonymously in 1694, part II in 1697; the proposal attracted the attention of Princess Anne of Denmark and provoked the suspicion that Astell was a crypto-Catholic.
literary_significance: The first systematic argument for women's education in English and a founding text of English feminism; its proposal for a female intellectual community anticipates later educational reform.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously as 'A Lover of Her Sex'; attribution to Astell is established.
bibliographical_notes: Part I 1694; Part II 1697. Standard edition: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies (Patricia Springborg, ed., Pickering & Chatto, 1997); also The First English Feminist: Reflections upon Marriage and Other Writings by Mary Astell (Bridget Hill, ed., 1986).

title: Some Reflections upon Marriage, Occasion'd by the Duke and Duchess of Mazarine's Case
description: Astell's second major feminist work, written in response to the scandalous separation of the Duke and Duchess of Mazarin, arguing that the legal subjection of wives is a form of arbitrary power inconsistent with the principles of the Glorious Revolution.
plot_or_argument: Astell asks how it can be that all men are born free, yet every woman is born a slave; she argues that marriage as constituted gives husbands arbitrary power over wives, that women must cultivate their reason, and that a rational education would make better wives and mothers.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in three parts with a preface to the third edition of 1706.
principal_characters: the Duchess of Mazarin; Hortense Mancini (alluded to)
meter_and_prosody: Ironical, pointed prose with a sustained rhetorical question.
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1700, with second and third editions in 1703 and 1706; the Mazarin case was a cause célèbre in Restoration and post-Revolution London.
literary_significance: One of the most powerful early feminist critiques of marriage and of the sexual double standard; its argument that arbitrary power over women is inconsistent with the principles of 1688 has made it a canonical text of political theory.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; attribution to Astell is established.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1700; third edition 1706. Standard edition: Some Reflections upon Marriage (Bridget Hill, ed., 1986); Political Writings (Patricia Springborg, ed., Broadview, 2002).

title: The Vanity of Dogmatizing; or, Confidence in Philosophy
description: Joseph Glanvill's sceptical defence of the new philosophy, which attacks Aristotelian scholastic dogmatism and argues that only experimental enquiry can extend knowledge; it was revised in 1665 as Scepsis Scientifica.
plot_or_argument: Glanvill argues that human understanding is weak and prone to error, that the schools' dogmatism is vain, and that the experimental method of Bacon and the Royal Society offers the only path to reliable knowledge; the work contains the famous witchcraft narrative of the Drummer of Tedworth.
narrative_structure: A series of chapters of sceptical argument with illustrative narratives.
meter_and_prosody: Elegant, persuasive prose admired by the Royal Society.
historical_context: Published in 1661, a year before the Royal Society's charter; Glanvill became a Fellow in 1664 and one of its most eloquent apologists.
literary_significance: The most readable early statement of the case for experimental philosophy in English and a source for the sceptical tradition that influenced Hume; the 1665 revision Scepsis Scientifica was widely read.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Glanvill; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1661 as The Vanity of Dogmatizing; revised 1665 as Scepsis Scientifica. Standard edition: Scepsis Scientifica (F. I. MacKinnon, ed., 1931); Essays of Joseph Glanvill (F. I. MacKinnon, ed., 1937).

title: The Discovery of a World in the Moone; or, A Discourse Tending to Prove That 'Tis Probable There May Be Another Habitable World in That Planet
alternative_titles: The Discovery of a World in the Moone
description: John Wilkins's popular scientific treatise arguing, on Copernican grounds, that the moon is probably a habitable world, with a discussion of the possibility of flight to it; it introduced the new astronomy to a general English readership.
plot_or_argument: Wilkins argues that the earth is a planet, that the moon is an earth, and that it is probable the moon is inhabited; the final proposition considers whether flying to the moon might one day be possible.
narrative_structure: A series of numbered propositions with arguments and objections answered.
meter_and_prosody: Clear, persuasive prose for a lay readership.
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1638 by the young Wadham College fellow who would become a founder of the Royal Society; it drew on Galileo, Kepler, and Godwin's The Man in the Moone.
literary_significance: The first popular English exposition of the plurality of worlds and a major influence on seventeenth-century imaginative literature, including Milton's cosmology and the early science fiction of Cyrano de Bergerac.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously; Wilkins's authorship was acknowledged in the third edition of 1684.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1638; third edition 1684 with A Discourse Concerning a New Planet. Standard edition: The Discovery of a World in the Moone (John Wilkins, London, 1638), in John Wilkins, Mathematical Magick (1648).

title: An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language
alternative_titles: An Essay towards a Real Character
description: Wilkins's ambitious scheme for a universal philosophical language in which the characters would correspond directly to the things and ideas they signify, with a full classification of knowledge as its foundation.
plot_or_argument: Wilkins proposes a 'real character' — a written symbol system independent of any natural language — and a taxonomic arrangement of all ideas into genera and species, so that the language would itself be a philosophy.
narrative_structure: Four parts: the design of the character, the philosophical tables, the grammar, and a vocabulary.
meter_and_prosody: Systematic technical prose with extensive tables.
historical_context: Published in 1668 for the Royal Society, of which Wilkins was a founding fellow and first secretary; it belongs to the seventeenth-century quest for a universal language.
literary_significance: The most elaborate of the seventeenth-century universal-language projects and a landmark in the history of taxonomy, semiotics, and information science; it influenced Leibniz and later classification systems.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Wilkins; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1668 (Royal Society). Standard edition: An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language (facsimile, Scolar Press, 1968); discussed in Umberto Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1995).

title: The History of the Royal-Society of London for Improving of Natural Knowledge
description: Thomas Sprat's official history of the Royal Society, commissioned by the Society itself, which defends the new experimental philosophy against its critics and sets out the ideal of a plain, unadorned prose suited to the reporting of fact.
plot_or_argument: Part I surveys the history of learning and the corruption of philosophy; part II describes the Society's constitution, methods, and achievements; part III answers the objections of the schools, the wits, and the clergy.
narrative_structure: Three parts in a continuous history and defence.
principal_characters: Francis Bacon; Charles II; the Fellows of the Royal Society
meter_and_prosody: Elegant but plain prose; the famous passage on the Society's resolution to reject 'swelling of style' and to use 'a close, naked, natural way of speaking' became the manifesto of the plain style.
historical_context: Published in 1667, five years after the Society's charter; Sprat was a chaplain and Fellow who had access to the Society's records and to Evelyn and Wren.
literary_significance: The principal source for the early history of the Royal Society and the classic statement of the ideal of plain prose that dominated English non-fiction for a century; it has been a touchstone in the history of scientific writing.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Sprat; the work was commissioned and corrected by the Society.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1667. Standard edition: The History of the Royal Society of London (J. I. Cope and H. W. Jones, eds., Routledge & Kegan Paul / Washington University Press, 1958).

title: Micrographia: or, Some Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by Magnifying Glasses
description: Robert Hooke's account of his observations through the compound microscope, published by the Royal Society in 1665 with fifty-seven magnificent engraved plates, in which he first used the word 'cell' for the units of plant tissue.
plot_or_argument: Hooke describes and illustrates the point of a needle, the edge of a razor, silk, cork, charcoal, moss, nettles, insects including the fly's eye and the flea, the moon, and the stars, arguing that microscopy reveals a hidden order in nature.
narrative_structure: A series of numbered observations, each with an engraved plate and a commentary.
literary_form: scientific treatise; natural history; illustrated book
meter_and_prosody: Precise descriptive prose; the plates by Hooke himself are among the finest scientific illustrations ever made.
historical_context: Published in September 1665 by the Royal Society; it was the first major publication of the Society and a sensation at court, where Pepys recorded it as 'the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life'.
literary_significance: The founding work of microscopy and of cell biology; the word 'cell' originates here, and its plates created the visual language of modern science.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Hooke; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1665 (Royal Society, London). Standard edition: Micrographia (facsimile, Dover, 2003); Robert Hooke, Micrographia (Michael Hunter, ed.).

title: Enthusiasmus Triumphatus; or, A Brief Account of the Nature, Causes, Kinds, and Cure of Enthusiasm
description: Henry More's influential analysis of religious enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination, published in his Collection of Several Philosophical Writings and directed against the sectarian excesses of the Commonwealth.
plot_or_argument: More identifies enthusiasm with the disturbance of the animal spirits, with melancholy, with ignorance, and with the pride of private revelation, and proposes reason, self-examination, and the discipline of the church as its cure.
narrative_structure: A single treatise in sections.
meter_and_prosody: Learned, argumentative prose.
historical_context: Published in 1656 during the Commonwealth, when the sects proliferated; More was a Cambridge Platonist concerned to defend a rational Christianity against both enthusiasm and materialism.
literary_significance: The standard seventeenth-century treatment of enthusiasm and a key text in the history of the psychology of religion; it influenced Shaftesbury, Swift's Tale of a Tub, and the eighteenth-century debate on fanaticism.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Henry More; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published in A Collection of Several Philosophical Writings (1662), having appeared in 1656. Standard edition: The Philosophical Writings of Henry More (Alexander Balmain Bruce, ed., 1925).

title: The True Intellectual System of the Universe
description: Ralph Cudworth's massive learned work against atheism, in which he argues that the ancient philosophers were not atheists and that a rational theism is the true intellectual system of the universe.
plot_or_argument: Book I sets out the various forms of atheism and refutes them; the work argues for the existence of plastic natures, for the immateriality of the soul, and for the eternity of moral truths against Hobbesian materialism.
narrative_structure: A single vast treatise in four books (only the first volume was published), with enormous learned apparatus.
meter_and_prosody: Dense, heavily cited scholarly prose of the Cambridge Platonists.
historical_context: Published in 1678, the year of the Popish Plot, and licensed by Samuel Parker; Cudworth was Master of Christ's College, Cambridge.
literary_significance: The most learned philosophical work of the seventeenth-century English Platonists; its concept of 'plastic nature' influenced Leibniz and later vitalist philosophy, and its refutation of atheism was a standard reference.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Cudworth; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1678 (London). Standard edition: The True Intellectual System of the Universe (John Harrison, ed., 3 vols., 1978); also in the Garland facsimile of 1978.

title: The Commonwealth of Oceana
description: James Harrington's utopian treatise on the ideal commonwealth, in which he argues that political power follows the distribution of landed property and proposes an elaborate republican constitution with a bicameral legislature and rotation of office.
plot_or_argument: The Archon of Oceana, after the dissolution of the old government, establishes a commonwealth founded on an agrarian law limiting landed property, with a Senate proposing, a popular assembly resolving, and a magistracy executing; the model is Venice and ancient republics rather than monarchy.
narrative_structure: A narrative frame of the founding of Oceana followed by the text of the proposed constitution and the Model of the Commonwealth.
principal_characters: the Archon; Olphaus Megaletor; the Council of Legislators; Parthenia
meter_and_prosody: A mixture of narrative and constitutional prose.
historical_context: Written during the Protectorate and dedicated to Cromwell, who is said to have suppressed it until Harrington's friends obtained its release; published in 1656.
literary_significance: The most original political theory of the Interregnum; its theory that power follows property influenced Marx, and its constitutional model directly shaped the constitutions of the American colonies and of the early United States.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Harrington; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1656. Standard edition: The Political Works of James Harrington (J. G. A. Pocock, ed., Cambridge University Press, 1977); Oceana (S. B. Liljegren, ed., 1924).

title: The Law of Freedom in a Platform; or, True Magistracy Restored
description: Winstanley's mature political programme, addressed to Cromwell, in which he sets out the constitution of a free commonwealth without buying, selling, or private land, and with an elected magistracy and universal education.
plot_or_argument: Winstanley proposes a commonwealth in which the earth is a common treasury, labour is organised communally, the clergy of the old order are abolished, magistrates are elected annually by the people, and laws are short, plain, and enforced by storehouses and officers.
narrative_structure: Six chapters with a dedicatory epistle to Cromwell and a proposed code of laws.
meter_and_prosody: Prophetic, plain, biblical prose of the radical sects.
historical_context: Published in 1652, three years after the Diggers' experiment on St George's Hill (1649), and dedicated to Cromwell, whose commonwealth Winstanley urged to go further.
literary_significance: The fullest statement of English Digger communism and one of the most original political documents of the seventeenth century; it anticipates socialist and anarchist thought and has been a touchstone for the radical tradition.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Winstanley; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1652. Standard edition: The Complete Works of Gerrard Winstanley (Thomas Corns, Ann Hughes, and David Loewenstein, eds., Oxford University Press, 2009), 2 vols.

title: The New Law of Righteousness
description: Winstanley's principal theological and political manifesto, published in January 1649, which argues that private property is the origin of oppression and that the restoration of the earth as a common treasury is the true law of righteousness.
plot_or_argument: Winstanley identifies the curse of Cain with the enclosure of the earth, argues that Christ's kingdom is a commonwealth of shared labour and property, and calls for the abolition of buying and selling.
narrative_structure: A single continuous argument in biblical and prophetic prose.
meter_and_prosody: Vigorous, scriptural prose of the radical sects.
historical_context: Published in January 1649, days before the execution of Charles I; it prepared the ground for the Digger settlement on St George's Hill in April 1649.
literary_significance: The founding text of English agrarian communism and an essential document of the radical revolution of 1649.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Winstanley; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1649. Standard edition: The Complete Works of Gerrard Winstanley (Oxford University Press, 2009).

title: England's Birth-Right Justified
alternative_titles: England's Birth-Right Justified Against All Arbitrary Usurpation
description: John Lilburne's principal Leveller pamphlet, in which he claims that the free-born people of England possess an inalienable birth-right of liberty that no parliament or king may take away.
plot_or_argument: Lilburne argues that arbitrary imprisonment, taxation without consent, the monopoly of the law, and the power of the great are all violations of the birth-right of every free-born Englishman, and that the people's representatives must be accountable.
narrative_structure: A single polemical tract with a dedicatory epistle.
meter_and_prosody: Fierce, urgent, colloquial prose of the pamphlet wars.
historical_context: Published in October 1645 during the civil wars, while Lilburne was serving in the parliamentary army; it laid the intellectual foundations of the Leveller movement.
literary_significance: A foundational text of English radicalism and of the doctrine of popular sovereignty; its language of birth-right influenced the Leveller Agreements and, through them, later democratic theory.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Lilburne; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1645. Standard edition: The English Levellers (Andrew Sharp, ed., Cambridge University Press, 1998); Freeborn John: The Complete Works of John Lilburne (2007- ).

title: Sermons upon Several Occasions (Tillotson)
alternative_titles: The Works of the Most Reverend Dr John Tillotson
description: The collected sermons of John Tillotson, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1691, published posthumously by his chaplain Ralph Barker; they are the model of latitudinarian preaching and were among the most widely read religious works of the eighteenth century.
plot_or_argument: The sermons expound a rational, moral, and tolerant Christianity: the reasonableness of revelation, the duties of charity and justice, the evil of strife and persecution, and the practical character of true religion.
narrative_structure: A collection of occasional sermons arranged by subject and occasion.
meter_and_prosody: Clear, balanced, plain prose that became the standard of English pulpit eloquence.
historical_context: Tillotson preached at St Lawrence Jewry and at court through the Restoration and after the Revolution; he was made Archbishop of Canterbury in 1691 and died in 1694; the folio of his Works appeared in 1696.
literary_significance: Tillotson's sermons defined latitudinarian prose style and were a principal influence on Addison, Swift's models of plain preaching, and the moral temper of eighteenth-century Anglicanism.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Tillotson; the posthumous collection was edited by Ralph Barker.
bibliographical_notes: First collected 1696 (The Works of the Most Reverend Dr John Tillotson, 3 vols. folio). Standard edition: The Works of John Tillotson (1757), 12 vols.; also Tillotson, Sermons (Oxford, 1820).

title: The History of the Reformation of the Church of England
description: Gilbert Burnet's monumental church history in three volumes (1679, 1681, 1714), which gave the Church of England an authoritative narrative of its separation from Rome and became the standard Protestant account of the Reformation.
plot_or_argument: Burnet narrates the reigns of Henry VIII, Edward VI, and Elizabeth I, using original documents, to show the Reformation as a lawful and providential return to primitive Christianity.
narrative_structure: Three volumes of narrative history with collections of documents appended.
principal_characters: Henry VIII; Thomas Cranmer; Edward VI; Elizabeth I; Thomas Cromwell; Thomas More
meter_and_prosody: Clear, vigorous, plain historical prose.
historical_context: Volume I published in 1679 and rewarded with a doctorate of divinity by Oxford; volume II in 1681 and volume III, posthumously, in 1714.
literary_significance: The standard English history of the Reformation for two centuries and a principal source for the Anglican identity of the Church of England.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Burnet; authorship undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: Volumes I-III published 1679, 1681, 1714. Standard edition: The History of the Reformation of the Church of England (N. Pocock, ed., Oxford, 1865), 7 vols.

title: Bishop Burnet's History of His Own Time
description: Burnet's posthumous history of England from the Restoration to the Treaty of Utrecht, written from his own experience as a bishop and courtier and published in two volumes in 1724 and 1734.
plot_or_argument: The history narrates the reigns of Charles II, James II, William III, and Anne, with candid portraits of the leading statesmen and a Whig interpretation of the Revolution.
narrative_structure: Two volumes covering 1660 to 1713, with digressions on the reigns before.
principal_characters: Charles II; James II; William III; Anne; Shaftesbury; Clarendon; Halifax; Rochester
meter_and_prosody: Lively, anecdotal, sometimes careless prose of a participant historian.
historical_context: Written from 1683 until Burnet's death in 1715; published by his son Thomas in 1724 and 1734.
literary_significance: One of the most important primary sources for the history of Restoration and Revolution politics; its portraits and anecdotes were widely quoted by Macaulay and later historians.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Burnet; published posthumously by his son.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1724 (vol. I) and 1734 (vol. II). Standard edition: Bishop Burnet's History of His Own Time (M. J. Routh, ed., Oxford, 1833), 6 vols.
